articles.title: ‘Like a Bond villain’s lair’: I climbed the Dolomites to the world’s most spectacular mountain hut
articles.summary: Perched above the clouds in northern Italy, Santnerpass refuge doesn’t just look stunning. It’s a marvel of eco-building – and vegetarian cuisine. ‘I think my boots are falling apart!” shouts Nigel just as we hit the pinnacles, a whole range of them jutting up and out from the mountainside, all…
body: I know how Nigel’s boots are feeling: the going is far harder than I was expecting. This is only the first day of our annual trip to the Dolomites, a vast range of breathtaking sawtooth peaks in northern Italy, but my head’s already full of the thought I have every year as we start out: “If only you’d got fitter.”

But it should be worth all the scrapes, bumps, scares and sweat. Somewhere up ahead, hopefully not too far, is Rifugio Passo Santner, or Santnerpass Hut, a spectacular mountain refuge that, as everyone who sits near my desk at work knows, has been obsessing me ever since I first saw a picture of it eight months ago.

Allowing you to stay deep in the mountains for days on end, the high-altitude Dolomites huts we overnight at all have their charms, from hearty food to giddying views to a generous way with the grappa. But in terms of appearance, they tend to fall into two not particularly pulse-quickening camps: stone block or cuckoo clock. Although you’re almost always overjoyed to see them, none could ever pass for a Bond villain’s lair, however much grappa you’ve had.

articles.title: Experience: I survived being buried in an avalanche
articles.summary: I was at the mercy of the mountain, heading towards a 20-metre drop, about to discover what it felt like to die. Growing up in Sweden, I was as comfortable on skis as I was walking on my feet. As a teenager, I became a professional free skier, a style that features jumps and tricks.
body: In March this year, we’d been staying at the base of the Lyngen Alps, northern Norway. Nonstop rain had prevented us from filming but, finally, we had fresh powder and clear skies. The plan was for me to go up the mountain with a friend, Lovisa, and make our way down as the sun was setting. Sofia would film us from the bottom using a drone.
We climbed to the summit, arriving just before sunset, but it was cloaked in cloud. I was disappointed. I was hooked up to audio and ready to go.

I suggested we ski down anyway, just for fun. I dug into the snow to make sure it was stable. If it’s not, the top layer of snow slides off the icier layer underneath. It didn’t move, so we took turns to zigzag slowly down, with me in the lead. Once we broke through the clouds, we had breathtaking views of the orange skies and blue fjords.
Then a dark line shot out from under my skis, a deep crack in the surface. I knew what it meant. My movement had caused a slab of snow to break away beneath me. I’d triggered an avalanche.

articles.title: There’s a long history of athletes pooing themselves mid-race – why, and how can you avoid it?
articles.summary: Since the ancient Olympics, athletes like Hyrox competitor Joanna Wietrzyk have experienced runner’s diarrhoea. What does the science say about extreme exercise’s ‘mechanical jostling of the intestines’? Soiling yourself in public sounds like a bad dream.
body: Wietrzyk won the fitness race but not before using communal equipment with faecal matter visibly running down her legs – and muddying Hyrox’s reputation.

Apologies aside, Wietrzyk’s unfortunate case of runner’s trots, or runner’s diarrhoea, is far more common than many people realise, throwing a new light on the ominous rows of portable toilets stationed along the course of a fun run and the knowing nods between runners as they pass them (or not).

About 60% of endurance athletes report some type of gastrointestinal symptoms during training or competition, according to Kayla Henningsen, a PhD candidate researching exercise gastroenterology and extremes physiology at Monash University. The American Medical Society for Sports Medicine estimates that the prevalence could be as high as 90%.

Severity varies considerably. “Symptoms can range from mild bloating and cramping through to nausea, diarrhoea and, in rare cases, loss of bowel control,” Henningsen says. “High-intensity events such as marathons, ultramarathons and Hyrox can create the perfect conditions for gastrointestinal distress, urgency or diarrhoea.”

articles.title: “I Don’t Want to Be Too Cool for School”: M&S CEO Stuart Machin on Its Fashion Turnaround
articles.summary: British high street retailer M&S is staging its debut show at London Fashion Week on Friday. While fashion insiders love its new output, internally, the business has a long way to go.
body: Ask a Brit their thoughts on retailer Marks & Spencer, proudly nicknamed Marks & Sparks or M&S, and many of them will express some level of fondness. They may like the Percy Pig sweets, regularly grab a sandwich meal deal, or test out the ever-growing list of viral products, like the Reggiano Lambrusco sparkling red wine.

But as of late, it’s not just M&S food (and now-viral director of product development, Kathryn Turner ) that’s prompting buzz. M&S fashion has upped its game in recent years, under chief executive Stuart Machin, who was appointed in 2022, and is in the middle of a major turnaround spanning product, supply chain, marketing and more.

To underscore its fashion ambitions, M&S will make its runway debut at London Fashion Week this Friday. The see-now, buy-now show, focused on its Fall/Winter 2026 collection, will feature reworkings of archival hits, while the diverse casting will reflect M&S campaigns, consumers and brand ambassadors. Crucially, half of the collection is under £50.
Pieces in the see-now-buy-now show (teased here) will reference popular archival pieces from M&S’s history, bringing them into the modern day. Half the collection will be under £50.

articles.title: TWP’s Path From Best-Kept Secret to Serious Fashion Player
articles.summary: In the midst of a store opening tear, TWP co-founders Trish Wescoat Pound and Andrew Rosen break down the brand’s speedy rise into fashion’s mainstream.
body: To track TWP’s rise from insidery fashion label to mainstream player, look to the real estate.

In August, the downtown New York ready-to-wear brand moved into its new headquarters at 21 Howard Street, having purchased the building to house its offices, showroom, manufacturing and design — all of which will be fully realized by 2027. To celebrate the new digs, it hosted its Spring/Summer 2027 show at the HQ’s bottom floor on day one of New York Fashion Week. The sweeping space felt like an arrival for the 2021-founded label, which debuted on the calendar with a small showing at Fouquet’s only a few seasons ago, in 2024.

Then, there are the stores. TWP opened its first outpost in London in August, before its second location on New York’s Madison Avenue in September, bringing its store count to 12. Five more will open by the end of the year, meaning in 2026 alone, TWP will have doubled its store count, hitting 17 stores, up from seven stores the year prior.
points: In the midst of a store opening tear, TWP co-founders Trish Wescoat Pound and Andrew Rosen break down the brand’s speedy rise into fashion’s mainstream.

articles.title: “Stopping Was Not the Answer”: Fashion Week in a Political Crisis
articles.summary: From Kyiv to Tbilisi and Dubai, organizers are producing globally recognized fashion weeks despite instabilities. For designers, it’s a business lifeline.
body: Just days before Ukrainian Fashion Week Spring/Summer 2027 began, Russian air strikes intensified on the city of Kyiv. The schedule, which ran from September 2-6, continued with strict safety protocols. Any time an air raid alert sounded, events were suspended immediately as guests, designers, and teams took shelter. Three shows — Viktor Anisimov, Darja Donezz, and Vorozhbyt & Zemskova — took place inside allocated bomb shelters near their venues. Five alerts sounded during a business conference, with guests and speakers leaving and returning after the all-clear, each time. Heroically, 50 brands managed to show against the odds.

“We all live and work within the same reality, and there is a strong shared understanding of the context,” says Iryna Danylevska, founder of Ukrainian Fashion Week. “Nevertheless, of the five wartime seasons we’ve held in Ukraine, this 59th season was by far the most demanding, while also becoming truly historic — both for the Ukrainian fashion industry and in the broader context of the global fashion week experience.”
points: From Kyiv to Tbilisi and Dubai, organizers are producing globally recognized fashion weeks despite instabilities.

articles.title: Why Nick Knight Used AI to Create H&M’s Interactive Show
articles.summary: The photographer turned studio stills into AI-generated fashion films for H&M’s latest London Fashion Week show. Here, he and H&M’s creative director explain why they’re experimenting with a technology that still divides fashion.
body: Fashion is still figuring out how comfortable it is with AI-generated imagery. Experiments with the tech raise thorny questions over everything from copyright and creative authorship to the future of models, photographers and other image-makers. At London Fashion Week last night, H&M stepped directly into that debate (as well as further into the wool debate, when Peta protestors crashed the show).

For its Fall/Winter 2027 show, titled H&M&YOU&I, the Swedish retailer enlisted photographer Nick Knight and SHOWstudio to create a one-off AI-powered interactive that turned still photography and illustration into fashion films generated in real time, which models and guests could influence by moving in front of them as the show unfolded.

“Fashion imagery can feel distant, and this project is about human connections and relationships in a digital age,” says Jörgen Andersson, H&M’s global creative director. “I think we all move between the physical and digital constantly – it is a reality of modern life. So with this show, we wanted to reflect that, all while offering a vision of fashion and the fashion show that is artistic, experimental, painterly and beautiful.”

articles.title: 11 Scenic Train Rides in the US Worth Booking for the Views Alone
articles.summary: From Amtrak routes along California’s coast to the wild beauty of the Alaska Railroad, the best way to see the vast natural beauty of the US is by train.
body: Every year, instead of flying home to southeastern Virginia, I always opt to take the train.

My journey typically starts in New York, winding down the Northeast Corridor before stopping in Washington, DC. While this busy stretch of track is far from the most scenic train ride in the US, there were still moments when I found my face pressed against the window—like near Havre de Grace, Maryland where the Susquehanna River widens—unable to look away. It was a reminder of how the joys of slow travel can sneak up on you, even in familiar places you may have traveled through countless times before.
